1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the kingside knight, adds a second guard to d5 and watches e4, so White cannot easily build a pawn centre. Black keeps the pawn structure open for now and gets a sound, flexible game; White decides how sharp it gets, from quiet development to a gambit for the initiative.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn, takes b5 from the knight and leaves the c8-bishop's diagonal open, so the bishop can come out before ...e6. It aims at a solid pawn structure. The cost is that the b8-knight loses c6 and usually goes to d7.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop, heading for French Defence structures, which 3.e4 transposes to. The price is the usual one in the French: the c8-bishop is shut in behind the e6-pawn. Black gets a solid, fairly closed game.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so ...c6 can no longer support d5. Sound but offbeat.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bf5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Alburt Defence
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop before ...e6 can shut it in. It becomes a target, though: White gains kingside space and time by harassing it with pawns. Sound but rarely played.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bg4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Anti-Veresov
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, but it becomes a target at once: 3.f3 attacks it and White builds a broad centre with the bishop's retreat. Black spends two moves on one piece and gives White the easier game.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 c5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Irish Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and offers the c-pawn. Taking it with the d-pawn gives up the centre, and Black aims to win the pawn back with a quick bishop; developing the c1-bishop and recapturing on d4 instead declines with a slight edge for White. Viable, but a rare and little-explored sideline.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Shaviliuk Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for space with ...d4, but White simply takes it: after 3.dxe5 d4 the knight steps to b5 and Black has too little for the pawn. The gambit is risky and leaves White with a clear edge.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Veresov Attack, Dutch System
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Sets up a Stonewall structure, with the pawns on d5 and f5 holding e4. The price is a weak e5-square and an open e8-h5 diagonal, and 3.e4 fxe4 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxd5 wins the pawn back at once. Playable but rare and risky.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for d5 or e4. White takes the centre and leads in development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Be6.strategy: Stands in front of the e-pawn, so neither ...e6 nor ...e5 can follow, and the f8-bishop can only come out by way of ...g6. White has the freer centre and more space.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Qd7.strategy: Blocks the c8-bishop and takes d7 from the b8-knight, a queen move that develops nothing and does nothing for the centre. White develops with the better centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early, where it is a target: 3.Nb5 hits it and c7, and 3.e4 dxe4 4.Nxe4 attacks it with tempo, leaving White ahead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Allows 3.Bxh6 gxh6, which doubles Black's h-pawns and breaks up the kingside, with only the bishop pair in return.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Takes b5 from the knight, but develops nothing and spends a tempo on a rim pawn. Nothing weakens, so it is sound, yet White is first to the centre and develops freely; second-rate.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rim pawn and gives up control of b6, without helping the centre or developing a piece. White takes the centre with 3.e4.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the c8-bishop but does nothing for d5, so White takes the centre with 3.e4 and gets more space and easier development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8 knight and opens the e8-h5 diagonal to the king, so 3.e4 breaks open the centre against a loosened position. Black falls behind in development with an exposed king: the move gives away far more than a tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the f8 bishop, a sound set-up, but it does nothing for d5, so White takes the centre with 3.e4 and develops faster. Playable, but second-rate.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from the c1 bishop, which costs nothing serious, but it spends a tempo on a rim pawn that develops nothing. Playable; White takes the centre and develops faster, which makes it second-rate.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 h5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Shropshire Defence
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rim pawn, though it keeps White's g-pawn from chasing a bishop to f5 and costs no material. It gives up control of g6 and develops nothing, so White simply develops: playable, but second-rate.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5 as well as the c8-bishop, and nothing else guards the pawn, so 3.Nxd5 wins it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5, which has no other guard, so 3.Nxd5 wins a pawn. The bishop also takes d7 from the b8-knight.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bh3.strategy: Hangs the bishop to 3.gxh3, with no compensation at all.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.Nxd5 wins a pawn, and the king on d7 also shuts in the c8-bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Drops a pawn to 3.Nxb5. Black has nothing to regain it with: 3...Ba6 is met by 4.Nc3, and White keeps the extra pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Drops a pawn to 3.Bxg5 and weakens the whole kingside for nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Bf4.name: Rapport-Jobava System, with e6
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 can shut it in, eyeing c7 and e5. White pairs it with the knight on c3 to build an active set-up, while Black, with e6 played, has a solid but slightly passive light-squared bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4.strategy: Takes the full centre at once. White gets space and freer development, while Black has a solid position, a cramped light-squared bishop and the job of undermining the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, controls e5 and keeps the choice of set-up open. Solid and flexible, but less ambitious than the immediate central strike, and it leaves White to decide later what kind of game to play.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5 3.e4.name: Dutch Defence: Kingfisher Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5 3.e4.strategy: A pawn gambit that opens the centre at once to exploit the loosened kingside and a lead in development. Black can take the pawn, but must then develop carefully, and White gets real play for it. Sound but second-rate: it gives up a pawn where simple development keeps a small edge.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5 3.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, eyeing c7 and, with the d-pawn, controlling e5, the square Black's f-pawn has left behind. White gets comfortable development while Black's kingside is loosened.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, keeps d4 solid and fights for e5 in the long run. Sound and flexible, if less pointed than putting the bishop on the active diagonal first.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5.name: Richter-Veresov Attack
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5.background: Named after Kurt Richter, who developed new ideas in it in the 1930s, and Gavriil Veresov, who strengthened its theory and practice from the Second World War to the 1960s. Tartakower had played it regularly in the 1920s. It has never been very popular at the top level.
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and threatens Bxf6 to damage Black's pawn structure, so Black must decide how to meet the trade. White has put the queenside pieces first and plays for long castling and a central pawn push: an aggressive, offbeat system, sound but no way to claim an advantage.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4.name: Rapport-Jobava System
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4.background: A modern development of the London System named after the grandmasters Richárd Rapport and Baadur Jobava, combining Bf4 with Nc3.
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and points it at c7, which makes Nb5 a real threat: with bishop and knight both aiming at c7, the pawn would fall unless Black prepares. A good surprise weapon with attacking chances that is at worst roughly equal.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Qd3.name: Amazon Attack: Siberian Attack
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Qd3.strategy: Guards d4 and keeps Black's bishop off f5, where it would simply hang to the queen. In return the queen blocks the f1-bishop and can be harassed by Black's knights, while White's development lags. An offbeat idea that costs more time than it gains.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Hübsch Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4.background: Hübsch, an amateur, surprised Savielly Tartakower with this gambit in 1922. Emil Diemer used it to transpose into his favourite Blackmar-Diemer Gambit.
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4.strategy: A pawn sacrifice: Black's d-pawn and knight both control e4, so White cannot win the pawn back by force, but it gets open lines and quick development in return. Black has to play accurately to keep the pawn, so it is playable, though White risks more than it gains.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and fights for e5 while leaving the c1-bishop's diagonal undecided. A flexible, solid choice that keeps the position quiet, at the price of the early pressure the bishop moves create.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 e6.name: Rapport-Jobava System
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 e6.strategy: Supports d5 with a solid pawn and opens the f8-bishop, a natural and sturdy way to develop. The weak point stays c7, which Bf4 and a knight on b5 can both attack, so Black has to guard it as soon as the knight arrives.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 g6.name: Rapport-Jobava System
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 g6.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto, but the bishop on g7 cannot help guard c7, the very pawn that Bf4 and a knight on b5 attack. Black has to find another defender for it, while White develops with threats.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once, while it is held only by the queen. If White supports it, Black trades the c-pawn for White's e-pawn and gets open lines against the centre. The c7 square stays a target for the bishop and a knight on b5, so Black still has to watch for a knight jump there.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 a6.strategy: Takes b5 away from the knight, which removes the Nb5 idea against c7 before it starts, and leaves the b8-knight free to develop towards the centre. A patient, prophylactic reply that spends a move on the edge pawn for a calm development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in, but it gives White a tempo-gaining pawn storm: with f3 in place, g4 drives the bishop back and gains space on the kingside.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7.strategy: Defends the f6-knight with the other knight, so Bxf6 no longer damages Black's pawns and would only give away the bishop pair. The cost is that the c8-bishop is shut in for the moment, so Black needs a few quiet moves to free the position.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5.name: Richter-Veresov Attack
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5.strategy: Brings the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before it can be shut in, and adds a third piece to the fight for e4. Black allows Bxf6 and doubled pawns, but the bishop pair makes up for that, so the game stays level.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once instead of dealing with the threat on f6, accepting that Bxf6 will damage Black's pawns. In return Black gets quick central pressure and a half-open g-file, but the broken kingside structure stays a long-term concern.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Ne4.name: Richter-Veresov Attack: Boyce Defence
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Ne4.strategy: Hits the bishop with the knight, but White simply trades it off, and recapturing with the d-pawn leaves an advanced pawn on e4 for White to attack. The damage is small, so it is sound, but White gets the easier game.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5 4.f3.name: Richter-Veresov Attack: Richter Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5 4.f3.background: Named after Kurt Richter, who usually continued with 4.f3 against 3...Bf5.
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5 4.f3.strategy: Supports e4 so that White can build a broad pawn centre and push the bishop and knight back. The price is a loosened kingside and the knight on g1 losing its best square, so White has to be sure the centre advance works.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5 4.Bxf6.name: Richter-Veresov Attack: Veresov Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5 4.Bxf6.background: Named after Gavriil Veresov, who usually played 4.Bxf6 against 3...Bf5.
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5 4.Bxf6.strategy: Takes the knight to double Black's f-pawns after the recapture. The doubled pawns are not a large weakness, since Black keeps the bishop pair, so White plays a slow positional game and tries to trade off the light-squared bishops.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Bf5 4.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop, which can trade off Black's active light-squared bishop. It leaves Black time to avoid the doubled pawns, so White gets a safe, slow game rather than a lasting pull.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.Bxf6.strategy: Takes the knight at once: whichever pawn recaptures, Black ends up with doubled f-pawns. White gives up the bishop for a knight to cause that structural damage, and accepts that Black gets the bishop pair in return.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop in a quiet way, keeping the capture on f6 in reserve. It does not force the structural damage that the immediate capture does, so Black is free to settle the centre as it likes.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and guards d4 a second time, keeping the capture on f6 in hand. It forces nothing: Black can take on d4 and open the c-file, and White has an ordinary game without pressure.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.Bxf6 gxf6.strategy: Recaptures with the g-pawn, which keeps the c-, d- and e-pawns in the centre and opens the g-file for the rook. The kingside is left with doubled f-pawns and an isolated h-pawn, a structural cost Black accepts for central control and the bishop pair.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.Bxf6 exf6.strategy: Recaptures with the e-pawn, so the g-pawn stays home to shelter the king and the f8-bishop is opened. The cost is that no pawn is left to support d5 from e6, so it is defended by the queen alone against the knight and White's coming e-pawn push.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.Bxf6 cxd4.strategy: Ignores the recapture and drops a piece: White takes the pawn on d4 with the bishop, which also escapes the two pawns that attacked it, and is a knight up for nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.Bxf6 gxf6 5.strategy: Attacks d5 a second time, so it is hit by the pawn and the knight and defended only by the queen. White tries to open the centre while Black's kingside pawns are damaged and Black's king is not yet safe.

Supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop, a patient plan: White keeps a healthy pawn centre and lets Black's broken kingside pawns tell in the long run. It gives up the quick central break, so Black has time to organise.
Develops the knight and guards d4, a quiet move. It does not hinder Black from winning space in the centre with the e-pawn, which the f6 pawn supports, so White has a sound but unambitious game.

Takes the pawn and removes the double attack on d5, which leaves White's d-pawn attacked by the c-pawn and the queen. The pawn on e4 has no defender and is attacked by the knight, so Black has to hold it or give it back.

Trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and attacks the knight, but White recaptures with the queen, which hits d5 a third time. Black has to take on e4 and trade queens or lose d5, and either way the king stays in the centre.

Supports d5 with a pawn and opens the f8 bishop, but it loses a pawn: after 6.exd5 exd5 7.dxc5 the d5 pawn is attacked by queen and knight and c5 cannot be held. Black has some activity for it, but not enough.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.Bxf6 gxf6 5.name: Richter-Veresov Attack: Malich Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 c5 4.Bxf6 gxf6 5.strategy: Pushes the pawn past c5 and cramps Black's queenside, but Black simply holds the extra pawn with ...f5. The attack on the damaged kingside is slow, and White is left a pawn down with too little in return.

Regains the pawn by taking on c5 instead of e4, which takes the d-pawn out of the attack by Black's c-pawn and queen. The knight still attacks the pawn on e4, which has no defender, and Black's doubled f-pawns stay a lasting weakness.

Regains the pawn, but leaves d4 attacked twice, by the c-pawn and the queen, and defended once, by the queen: Black takes it and is a pawn up. White has only the lead in development and the damaged kingside as compensation.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7 4.Nf3.name: Richter-Veresov Attack: Two Knights System
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the second knight and covers e5, fighting for the centre with pieces instead of an early pawn push. The set-up is quiet and flexible: the bishop stays on g5, and White decides the pawn structure and the side to castle later.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7 4.Qd2.strategy: Prepares long castling and the e-pawn advance, with the queen on a diagonal that also stands behind the bishop on g5. It commits the queen early but keeps the other pieces flexible, a set-up for an attack on the kingside.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7 4.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 to build a broad pawn centre. The cost is a loosened kingside and the knight on g1 losing its best square, so White has to be sure the central advance works before Black strikes at the bishop with ...h6.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7 4.Nf3 g6.name: Richter-Veresov Attack: Two Knights System, Grünfeld Defence
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7 4.Nf3 g6.strategy: Aims for a fianchetto, with the bishop on g7 pressing d4 and the long diagonal while the knights guard the centre. The cost is that the bishop on g5 can go to h6 and harass the f8-bishop, so Black must watch the dark squares around the kingside.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7 4.Nf3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn and opens the f8-bishop, a solid way to meet the two knights. The c8-bishop stays shut in behind the pawn chain for now, but Black gets a sound centre and a safe king.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 Nbd7 4.Nf3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with the c-pawn and opens a5 for the queen, where it would pin the knight on c3 against the king. A sturdy set-up, though the c8-bishop stays shut in behind the knight on d7 and the b7 pawn.
